opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. This is something I've thought about a lot. I wrote an essay a while back called "The Hardware Lottery," and the core idea is that a research idea often wins not because it's universally better than the alternatives, but because it happens to suit the hardware and software available at the time.

Deep learning is a great example. Many of the core ideas, like backpropagation and convolutional networks, existed for decades. Neural networks were largely written off through the eighties and nineties, partly because the general-purpose CPUs of that era just weren't well matched to the workload. What changed things wasn't primarily a new theoretical breakthrough. It was that GPUs, which were built for video games, turned out to be extraordinarily good at the matrix multiplications deep learning depends on. Suddenly an idea that had looked impractical became very practical, and it took off.

What worries me is that the lottery doesn't end there. Hardware is becoming more specialized, with accelerators tuned for dense matrix multiplication and the kinds of architectures we use today. That creates a feedback loop. The ideas that run well on current hardware get explored, they produce good results, which justifies building more hardware optimized for them. Meanwhile, ideas that might be just as promising, or more so, but that need sparsity, dynamic computation, or different memory access patterns, get left behind. That isn't because they failed on their merits. It's because they're expensive to try at all.

So the cost of straying from the beaten path keeps rising. If you're a researcher with a genuinely different idea, you have to fight the current software stack and the hardware, which means you're judged on an uneven playing field. Some of the ideas we've dismissed may simply have been tested on the wrong tools.

I don't think the answer is to stop specializing, because specialization brings huge efficiency gains. But we should be more aware that the tools we have shape which questions we ask. Investing in more flexible hardware, better software abstractions, and ways to lower the cost of exploring unconventional directions would help make sure the next big idea isn't held back just because it lost the lottery.

r001.rationale: The response says GPUs made deep learning workloads practical and helped the field take off, but it does not say they enabled substantially deeper neural networks.

r002.rationale: The response explains that ideas gain traction when available hardware and software make them practical, and may be overlooked when they are expensive to test with current tools.

r003.rationale: It notes that current accelerators favor dense matrix multiplication and that sparsity can be left behind, but does not attribute a lack of GPU performance gains from unstructured sparsity to reliance on structured matrix representations.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So the way I've come to think about it is that hardware is never neutral. We like to tell ourselves this story that ideas win in machine learning because they're good ideas, that there's some kind of meritocracy of algorithms. But if you actually look at the history, what wins is heavily determined by what the available hardware makes cheap to run. I ended up calling this "the hardware lottery," because it really does feel like a lottery: a research idea succeeds not necessarily because it's superior, but because it happens to be compatible with the software and hardware that already exist.

The classic example is deep learning itself. Backpropagation was around in the sixties and really worked out in the eighties. Convolutional networks existed in the late eighties and nineties. And yet those ideas basically lost for decades, because the general-purpose CPUs of that era were terrible at the kind of massively parallel matrix multiplication that neural networks need. Then GPUs come along, built for a completely different purpose, which was rendering video games, and suddenly the thing that was dismissed as a dead end becomes the dominant paradigm almost overnight. The idea didn't change. The hardware did.

What worries me is that we're now in a moment where this lottery is becoming much more pronounced rather than less. For a long time we had this kind of accidental generality, where the same CPU could run almost anything reasonably well, so a researcher with an unconventional idea could at least try it. Now the economics of chip design have pushed everyone toward specialization. We're building TPUs and accelerators that are exquisitely optimized for dense matrix multiplies on large models. That's fantastic if your idea looks like today's deep learning. It's a real problem if your idea looks different, say it's sparse, or event-driven, or needs a lot of branching. Those ideas aren't just slower to run, they're often orders of magnitude more expensive to even test, and so they quietly don't get explored. Nobody decides to kill them, they just never get a fair hearing.

And I think that's the subtle part. The cost of being on the wrong side of the hardware lottery used to be that you were a bit slower. Now the cost is that you may not get to run your experiment at all, because the entire stack, from the chip up through the frameworks, has been co-designed around a single narrow set of assumptions. So when people ask me how I understand the role of hardware, my honest answer is that it's acting as a very strong, mostly invisible filter on the space of ideas we take seriously. And I think as a field we should be a lot more deliberate about that, whether that means investing in more flexible hardware, better tooling for trying unconventional ideas, or just being more humble about what we think we've learned about which approaches "work."

r001.rationale: The response says GPUs made neural networks dominant by enabling massively parallel matrix multiplication, but it does not identify them as enabling substantially deeper networks.

r002.rationale: It says ideas gain success when they are compatible with available hardware and software, and that hardware determines which ideas become dominant.

r003.rationale: It notes that sparse ideas can be expensive to test, but does not attribute missing GPU performance gains from unstructured sparsity to reliance on structured matrix representations.

astra-6.text:
I think we often treat hardware as an implementation detail: you come up with an algorithm, and then you figure out how to run it. But hardware actually shapes which ideas we can explore in the first place. It determines how quickly you can run experiments, how much iteration you can do, and whether an approach is practical at scale.

If your idea maps well onto the operations that existing hardware accelerates, you have an enormous advantage. You can test it, improve it, and demonstrate results. An idea that doesn’t map well might look uncompetitive, even if the underlying approach is promising. So we have to be careful about interpreting what succeeds as purely a judgment about the quality of the algorithm.

There’s also a feedback loop. Hardware gets optimized for the approaches that are popular, and researchers gravitate toward approaches that run efficiently on that hardware. That can be incredibly productive, but it can also narrow the space of ideas we pursue. For me, the interesting question is: which ideas are we overlooking because we don’t yet have the right tools to give them a fair test?

sol-6.1.text:
I think we often treat hardware as something that comes after the research: you have an idea, and then you figure out how to run it. But hardware actually shapes which ideas we can explore in the first place. It determines how quickly you can experiment, how large you can scale, and whether other researchers can reproduce your results.

If an approach maps well onto the hardware we have, it gets a much easier path to demonstrating its potential. An approach that’s harder to run may look less promising simply because we haven’t been able to give it the same investment or experimentation. So there’s a feedback loop: we build hardware for popular algorithms, and then those algorithms become even more attractive because they run well on that hardware.

That doesn’t mean their success isn’t deserved. It means we should be careful about equating what’s efficient on today’s hardware with what’s fundamentally the best idea. The tools we have influence the research questions we ask—and sometimes the questions we don’t ask.
